entries.source: Chapter XLVIII asks whether a servant shall gain freedom from his master; it begins only after the divider separating Chapter XLVII.
pre: Historical horary question regarding service or slavery.
lim: Source social relation is from the 1647 text, not an endorsement or contemporary legal model.

entries.source: The first house, its lord and the Moon are assigned to signify the servant in this question.
pre: Use a chart erected for the question.
lim: These represent the servant; do not substitute the master's tenth-house lord.

entries.source: The tenth house and lord of its sign denote the master, whatever his social condition.
pre: Same service question and its tenth house.
lim: The author's 'let his condition be what it will' must not be collapsed into a class restriction.

entries.source: Examine joining of the ascendant's lord to the tenth lord and whether the author calls it a perfect conjunction, whether by body or aspect, with or without reception.
pre: Compare these two specific significators; evaluate body/aspect and reception independently.
lim: The text's broad use of 'conjunction ... by body or aspect' is retained without imposing a narrower modern technical definition.

entries.source: If the joining is exact by degree and minute, the servant is said to gain freedom easily and in a short time.
pre: The conjunction between first-house lord and tenth-house lord is perfect to degree and minute.
lim: Both exactness and the two designated lords matter; not every contact means immediate release.

entries.source: If the ascendant lord has separated from the tenth lord by only a few minutes, Lilly treats the servant as effectively freed already.
pre: A recent separation of a few minutes, not an applying conjunction.
lim: Source describes an inference from already separating geometry; does not document an actual release.

entries.source: If no such joining or aspect occurs between the two lords, apply the same method to the Moon as substitute servant significator.
pre: First lord–tenth lord contact is absent.
lim: The Moon must make the same relevant aspect; no automatic positive result from mere presence.

entries.source: If neither the Moon nor first-house lord separates from the tenth lord, Lilly next examines whether either separates from or joins the Sun, judging by similar aspect conditions.
pre: Both prior comparisons fail; distinguish separation from joining with the Sun.
lim: The source introduces a second fallback to Sun; not an unconditional 'Sun means freedom' rule.

entries.source: The text distinguishes a determinate from an absolute question and contrasts release from this particular master now with ever gaining freedom from his power.
pre: Identify whether the query concerns a specific current master or freedom more generally.
lim: The author's 'determinate and not absolute' phrasing is ambiguous with the paired examples and should be preserved, not silently repaired.

entries.source: For the specified question, a first-house lord cadent from an angle and lacking an aspect to the ascendant is given as a condition predicting departure from service.
pre: Source combines cadency from an angle with no ascendant aspect.
lim: Alternative source configurations follow; do not reclassify the whole preceding contact logic.

entries.source: A first-house lord in aspect to a planet occupying an angle, or with a planet that beholds the ascendant, is another configuration offered for gaining freedom.
pre: Planet in angle OR one that beholds ascendant; first lord aspect must exist.
lim: The phrase allows alternatives; no claim that a particular angular position alone proves the outcome.

entries.source: The first-house lord located in the third or ninth house, or joined to a planet in either, is offered as a sign the servant will depart.
pre: Third/ninth placement OR conjunction with a planet located there.
lim: These are alternative placements, not one obligatory composite aspect.

entries.source: The same departure reasoning is allowed from the Moon if its aspects supply the corresponding conditions.
pre: Moon must exhibit analogous aspects or configurations to those just listed.
lim: Do not count Moon and ascendant-lord as independent observed servant outcomes.

entries.source: If Moon or ascendant lord is in the ascendant, tenth, seventh or fourth, or joined to a planet in one of those angles, and that planet is direct, the servant is said not to be delivered.
pre: Specify Moon/ascendant lord or joined angular planet; the stated planetary directness is essential.
lim: The conditional starts at printed296 bottom and continues printed297; preserve all four angular houses.

entries.source: If that aforesaid angular planet is retrograde instead of direct, the text allows freedom but with slowness and difficulty.
pre: The same angular-planet scenario, with retrograde motion substituting for direct motion.
lim: This qualifies the previous negative; retrogradation changes direction and tempo, not proof of actual freedom.

entries.source: When the ascendant lord in the angles is impeded by corporeal conjunction with an ill planet, freedom from service is denied.
pre: Ascendant lord afflicted in 1st/10th/7th/4th by conjunction to malefic.
lim: The house and affliction conditions belong together; separate from the generic principle of angular proximity.

entries.source: In the same angular impediment clause, a square or opposition from an ill planet to the ascendant lord also denies release.
pre: Angular first-house lord; malefic square or opposition.
lim: Both adverse aspect kinds are alternatives within one historical prohibition.

entries.source: If the first-house lord in the stated angular context is entering combustion, Lilly also denies freedom from that service.
pre: Entering (applying to) combustion, not simply any Sun placement.
lim: The source says 'entring combustion'; current combust and entering combustion are not interchangeable.

entries.source: The phrase Finis Sexæ Domus marks the end of the sixth-house treatment immediately after XLVIII and before the seventh-house introduction.
pre: Structural source boundary on printed297.
lim: Not a new numbered house theory or separate servant success event.

entries.source: The unnumbered heading The Significations of the seventh House begins the next house-topic introduction.
pre: Starts below the end-of-sixth-house line and ornamental rule.
lim: The heading is NOT Chapter XLIX and is not one of the forty-three aphorisms.

entries.source: The seventh-house heading lists marriage, open enemies, lawsuits, controversies, contracts, wars, bargains, fugitives and thefts.
pre: Original seventh-house topic list is on printed297.
lim: This enumerates 1647 topics, not validated associations or distinct observations.

entries.source: Lilly says questions naturally belonging to the seventh house demand more consideration and are more difficult to judge than those of any other house.
pre: Applies to the seventh-house class of questions.
lim: This is an authorial methodological claim, not measured predictive difficulty.

entries.source: The author says this difficulty required a larger exposition of opinions from both ancient authorities and some modern practitioners.
pre: Rationale for the following enlarged material.
lim: No independently enumerated source citations supplied here; not a primary-source collation of the named people.

entries.source: The introduction announces forty-three significant aphorisms, said to illuminate seventh-house matters and the broader body of astrology.
pre: Announcement explicitly says forty-three and broad application.
lim: Do not conflate these forty-three general horary aphorisms with the earlier forty-three physician aphorisms in chapter XLIV.

entries.source: The separate unnumbered heading Aphorismes and Considerations for better judging any Horary Question introduces the 43 numbered rules.
pre: This heading occurs on PDF332/printed298 before aphorism 1.
lim: Treat as general horary advice and seventh-house prefatory material, not a new numbered Chapter.
